transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-07 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Darren Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Aurora - Head of AI), Rajiv Menon (Aurora - Eng Mgr), Sofia Ramirez (Aurora - Sec/Compliance)
Recording: auto
Links shared: Redwood model catalog deck https://redwood.ai/decks/aurora-health-models.pdf, benchmark spreadsheet (private) https://redwood.internal/benchmarks/aurora-32k.csv

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on model selection for clinical summarization and patient-facing multilingual assistants. Key constraints: 32k+ context for long clinical notes, multilingual (EN/ES/FR), strong security (SOC2, KMS, VPC), tool-calling for EHR plugs and function calls. Discussed tradeoffs hosted vs dedicated vs private, and candidate open models.

Topics:
- Current stack and pain points
- Context length needs and examples
- Multilingual support and hallucination concerns
- Tool-calling / function calling for EHR actions
- Deployment modes (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) and security
- Next steps and benchmarking

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intro, I m Maya, AE on the retail—sorry, Redwood inference team, and Darren is our SE. How're you all doing?
[00:18] Lena (Aurora): Hi Maya, good, thanks. We re excited — trying to pick a model strategy and whether we run hosted or dedicate or go private for HIPAA workloads.
[00:28] Darren (Redwood SE): Hey folks, quick note, I'll go deep on latency, batching, and the 32k context constraints later — happy to jump in.
[00:36] Rajiv (Aurora): Quick context from our side: ~100 engineers, using a mix of python microservices, vector DB (we re on Pinecone today but evaluating alternatives), and majority of data is clinical notes — variable length, sometimes 15–20k tokens per patient. Need summarization, question answering, and structured extraction with tool calls into our EHR via a function interface.
[00:58] Maya: Great, that s helpful. Sofia, wanted to loop you in for compliance caveats?
[01:04] Sofia (Aurora): Yes, HIPAA is primary. We need SOC2 evidence, ability to integrate with our KMS (Azure Key Vault for now), audit logs, and ideally VPC/private deployment options for production. Also data residency — some records must stay in the US.
[01:22] Maya: Perfect. Quick qualifier: are you leaning toward a fully private on‑prem cluster or a VPC/private deployment in cloud?
[01:28] Sofia: Prefer VPC first, on‑prem later if needed.
[01:33] Darren: Noted. On models — can you describe the expected inference throughput and latency SLOs?
[01:39] Rajiv: Throughput is modest now, maybe 20–50 concurrent sessions, but peak bursts could be 200. Latency: for patient-facing flows we want <2s for short responses, but for long‑form summarization we're ok with 8–12s if the model is big and more accurate. Cost is a big factor too.
[01:57] Lena: Also, multilingual — English and Spanish primarily, some French. And hallucination risk is critical because we re pulling from claims and free text.
[02:07] Maya: Ok, so the model picks have to balance context window, instruction adherence, multilingual prowess, and hallucination control. Common open model candidates are Llama variants, Mistral, Falcon, and open weights fine‑tuned for instruction following. Any initial model preferences?
[02:25] Rajiv: We d like to test both large-context models (like 32k+ capable) and smaller quantized models for cost. How does Redwood handle model variants and fallbacks?
[02:34] Darren: We have model catalog and runtime supports multiple variants. Smart routing can send short requests to cheap quantized variants and longer or sensitive ones to larger pinned models. For dedicated, you can pin a model to a GPU pool. For private, you control the deployment — same API. We also do prefix/KV cache to reduce token costs on repeated contexts.
[02:55] Lena: Could you clarify KV cache? I ve seen K V cash in some transcripts before — what s it actually doing?
[03:02] Darren: Sure — KV cache stores past key/value states across a session so if you re sending overlapping context or doing stepwise generation we don t re-compute prior tokens, which lowers latency and cost. For very long notes we also support chunking + retrieval with embeddings instead of feeding the entire doc into the model.
[03:20] Rajiv: On retrieval: we re using Pinecone today. Does Redwood have recommended vector DBs and integrations?
[03:26] Maya: We recommend a few — Pinecone, Milvus, or our in‑platform caching for simple cases. For production latency you often want a colocated vector DB in the same VPC/region. We can share best practices in the doc pack.
[03:40] Sofia: Security question — how do you handle encryption in transit and at rest, and can we use our Azure KMS?
[03:47] Darren: Yes you can use your KMS. For hosted customers we integrate with customer-managed KMS for key wrapping on private deployments; hosted API uses our managed keys by default but for enterprise we support BYOK (bring your own key). We have TLS everywhere and per-token audit logging with optional retention windows.
[04:05] Rajiv: Good. On models, when you say Llama variants, which sizes are customers actually using for 32k context?
[04:12] Darren: Typically for 32k they use Llama 2 70B or larger, or specialized long-context models that have been compiled with chunked attention kernels. There's also the newer Mistral long-context forks and some community Falcon checkpoints optimized for long seqs. For 64k needs, it's less common but supported via sharded runtime and more memory.
[04:33] Lena: We re worried about hallucinations in multi-step tool-calling — we need deterministic function calls when extracting a structured medication list, for example. How does Redwood help with tool-calling correctness?
[04:44] Maya: We support structured function calling (like OpenAI function calling) where the model returns a JSON payload and our runtime can validate schemas. You can also run a lightweight verifier step or a rules engine. For extra safety you can route those outputs to a smaller deterministic model or a validation lambda.
[05:00] Rajiv: Does function calling require network egress to external services, or can we keep it inside the VPC for private deployments?
[05:06] Darren: You can keep all function calls inside your VPC. For hosted we support encrypted webhook calls and can support private link / peering to avoid public egress.
[05:16] Speaker 1: [garbled] hey uh the billing question — is there a difference in tokenization across models that affects billing?
[05:24] Maya: Yes, tokenization differences can change effective token counts; we show effective token metrics in the Console and billing is normalized to tokens but we also provide per-model cost breakdowns so you can estimate.
[05:33] Lena: For our clinical notes, typical doc sizes are up to 20k tokens, but combined with history we reach ~32k. Would you recommend full context or RAG?
[05:43] Darren: For extraction tasks, RAG with chunking + embeddings often reduces hallucination because you ground the model. For global summarization across the whole record, long-context models with KV cache or tiled attention can be better but more costly. We suggest testing both: RAG for Q/A and long‑context for one‑shot summarization.
[05:58] Rajiv: What about multilingual—do you get consistent performance across Spanish and French?
[06:04] Darren: Model choice matters: some open models are trained primarily on English; others like some Mistral-based or specialized multilingual models perform better. We often evaluate with prompt‑engineering plus small supervised fine-tune or instruction tuning on your bilingual dataset.
[06:18] Maya: Quick demo offer — we can run a pilot where we provision dedicated capacity for a short run and benchmark three model candidates on your sanitized 32k sample. Darren can scope the perf tests.
[06:29] Rajiv: That d be ideal. Also curious about quantization and latency tradeoffs—can you get near real-time with quantized 4-bit models?
[06:36] Darren: Yes, with the right kernels and GPU selection, 4-bit quantized models can get close to half the memory and decent latency. But some instruction-following quality drops a little; we recommend a quantization-aware eval for your exact tasks.
[06:50] Lena: We re using older embeddings for search; does Redwood have an embeddings endpoint and storage?
[06:55] Maya: Yes — embeddings as a first-class API. You can store vectors in your own DB or Redwood can offer short-term cache. For long-term storage we'd still recommend a specialized vector DB.
[07:05] Sofia: About compliance — what's in the SOC2 scope? Do you support attestations for specific modules?
[07:11] Darren: We have SOC2 Type II for our platform. For Private deployments you get additional controls since the data plane sits in your VPC; we can provide the SOC2 report and a security whitepaper. We also support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit logs per account.
[07:25] Rajiv: Any public perf numbers for 32k summarization latency?
[07:31] Maya: We have internal benchmark numbers in the catalog; we ll share a spreadsheet. Numbers vary widely by model and GPU — for example, Llama 2 70B on A100 80G might be roughly 6–10s for 32k load and summarization, while smaller models with RAG can be faster. We'll include specifics in the benchmark run.
[07:52] Lena: On pricing, we re sensitive — can you do committed reserved capacity for Dedicated?
[07:58] Maya: Yes — Redwood Dedicated supports reserved GPU pools with discounts and burst capacity. We'll include committed pricing examples.
[08:06] Rajiv: For the pilot, what's the minimal setup we need to provide?
[08:10] Darren: Ideally: 1) sanitized sample dataset for benchmarking (you can obfuscate PII), 2) typical prompt templates, 3) list of success metrics (latency, accuracy/hallucination thresholds, cost per summary), and 4) security checklist for the VPC/credentials.
[08:25] Lena: We'll prepare that. Any gotchas around tokenization for Spanish medical terms?
[08:30] Darren: Spanish medical terms mostly tokenize fine but domain-specific abbreviations might split odd. We recommend including such examples in the eval prompts.
[08:38] Speaker 2: [inaudible] how do rollouts and canaries work?
[08:42] Maya: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts by model version, per-route or per-customer. You can do A/B tests across model variants and automatic fallback to cheaper models if SLOs are violated.
[08:55] Rajiv: If we go private, do we lose any Console features?
[08:59] Darren: No — the private control plane mirrors the Console; certain telemetry can be routed to your monitoring stack. The main difference is data plane isolation.
[09:09] Lena: For tool-calling, can you enforce schema validation server-side so the model's JSON is verified before calling the EHR API?
[09:15] Darren: Yes, runtime-level schema validation is supported; you can also have pre-check hooks. We can log call payloads for audit and replay.
[09:25] Sofia: On logging, can we redact PHI in logs?
[09:29] Darren: Yes, log redaction and retention policies are configurable. For HIPAA we typically set short retention and redaction for PII fields.
[09:39] Lena: Are there customers in the health space already?
[09:42] Maya: Yes, we have a handful of med-tech and clinical customers — can share redacted case studies and references after an NDA.
[09:49] Rajiv: Any constraints on GPUs in Dedicated — for performance, what do you recommend?
[09:55] Darren: For large models and 32k context, A100 80G is a common choice; for cost-sensitive we run quantized models on T4s or RTX A5000-type nodes with optimized kernels. We'll include recommended configs.
[10:07] Maya: Ok let's recap and set next steps.
[10:11] Maya: Action items — we ll send pricing and SOC2 docs, Darren will scope the pilot bench and run 3-model comparison, and Aurora will provide sanitized sample and success metrics.
[10:21] Sofia: Sounds good. When can you start the benchmark?
[10:24] Darren: If we get the sample by 2025-05-09, we can run and return numbers by 2025-05-14.
[10:30] Rajiv: Works for us.
[10:32] Lena: Also, could you include an example of function calling flow for extracting meds and creating a FHIR JSON?
[10:38] Maya: Yes, Darren will include an example schema and flow in the tech deep dive.
[10:44] Speaker 3: [background] thanks, bye.
[10:46] Maya: Thanks everyone, we ll follow up with materials by next week.
[10:50] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: medium — some speaker overlap and occasional misheard acronyms (e.g., K V cash = KV cache).

End of transcript.
